--- title: "Uncertainty, Priors, Simulation, and Experiments" --- Before we fit a model to data, we need to understand what it does. Model building is not a pipeline where you write the equations, press "fit," and read off the answer. It is a *dialogue* between you, the model, the data, and the decisions the model informs — a bargaining process over model complexity, the data available to constrain it, and the consequences of different intervention strategies. At each stage, you're asking a specific question and using simulation to answer it. Two kinds of uncertainty run through this entire workflow: - **Parameter uncertainty** — we don't know the "true" parameters. (The scare quotes are deliberate: epidemiological parameters are effective summaries of complex processes, not fixed properties of nature.) The transmission parameter $\beta$ might be 0.3 or 0.5, and the epidemic looks very different in each case. This uncertainty shrinks when we fit the model to data, but never disappears entirely. - **Process uncertainty** — even if we knew every parameter exactly, the epidemic is a stochastic process. Run the same model with the same parameters twice and you get different trajectories. This uncertainty is intrinsic to the system and cannot be reduced by collecting more data. A single simulation trajectory ignores both. When a decision-maker asks "should we vaccinate?" the answer depends on the *distribution* of outcomes under both sources of uncertainty, not on one arbitrary simulated future. Carrying both kinds of uncertainty forward — from model specification through simulation to the eventual policy comparison — is what separates rigorous analysis from storytelling with curves. The example files for this chapter are in [`examples/experiments/`](https://github.com/vsbuffalo/camdl-book/tree/main/examples/experiments). ## Priors — simulating from beliefs alone We don't need data to start learning about our model; in fact we *should not* bring data into the picture until we've interrogated and explored how the model interacts with our current or *prior* beliefs. The first step is to encode our prior beliefs about the parameters directly in the model file. It may seem strange to bring our beliefs explicitly into a scientific model, in light of the notion that science is "objective" and "data-driven." But the reality is that (1) every model is built on a foundation of many assumptions and beliefs, and (2) we implicitly encode "flat" or "uniform" priors for model parameters when we simply state the parameter bounds, or state parameters live on a logscale. These implicit priors can seem neutral and objective, but are actually quite strong, and can have a large influence on model inference and the conclusions we draw from it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## "Flat" priors are not uninformative A long tradition in Bayesian statistics has shown that uniform or "vague" priors carry more information than they appear to. [Jeffreys (1961)](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/theory-of-probability-9780198503682) first demonstrated that flat priors are not invariant under reparameterization — a uniform prior on $\beta$ is not uniform on $\log \beta$, so the choice of parameterization smuggles in information. [Jaynes (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511790423) developed this further, arguing that maximum entropy is the principled baseline precisely because uniform priors on arbitrary scales are not "uninformative." More recently, [Gelman (2006)](https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/taumain.pdf) showed that common "vague" prior specifications (like $\text{InverseGamma}(\epsilon, \epsilon)$ for variance parameters) are in fact highly informative, and [Gelman et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.3150/16-BEJ868) argued that a prior can only be understood in the context of the likelihood it will interact with — there is no prior that is unconditionally "uninformative." With enough data, the prior's influence vanishes — the posterior concentrates around the maximum likelihood estimate regardless of the prior (the [Bernstein–von Mises theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernstein%E2%80%93von_Mises_theorem)). So this isn't about priors dominating the analysis forever. It's about the regime where priors matter most: when data is scarce — early in an outbreak, with a novel pathogen, or under limited surveillance. In those settings, which are exactly when decisions are most urgent, encoding domain knowledge through thoughtful priors can mean the difference between useful model-informed decisions and misleading ones. ::: Recall the parameters block from [Building an SIR Model](getting-started.qmd); these had no priors — just types and bounds. Yet these encode substantive "flat" beliefs: `beta` is a rate between 0.05 and 1.0, `gamma` is a rate between 0.01 and 0.5. These bounds rule out certain epidemics. But bounds are coarse; they say "not impossible," not "what I actually believe". Usually we have more specific beliefs about parameters values, just based on the context of the infectious disease and transmission processes. Putting this prior information into the model file makes it visible and explicit. But more importantly, it *concentrates* our beliefs into a smaller region of plausible parameter space, which greatly improves how well inference works. camdl lets you attach a prior distribution directly to the parameter declaration using the `~` operator — standard "distributed as" notation from Bayesian modeling: ```camdl parameters { beta : rate in [0.05, 1.0] ~ log_normal(mu = -1.0, sigma = 0.5) gamma : rate in [0.01, 0.5] ~ half_normal(sigma = 0.5) rho : probability in [0.1, 0.9] ~ beta(alpha = 2.0, beta = 5.0) k : positive in [1.0, 100.0] ~ half_normal(sigma = 10.0) N0 : count # no prior — fixed externally I0 : count # no prior — fixed externally } ``` Each line now reads as a complete belief statement: `beta` is a rate, plausible between 0.05 and 1.0, with a log-normal prior centered around $e^{-1} \approx 0.37$. The type, bounds, and prior are all visible at the declaration --- a reader doesn't need to look anywhere else to understand what the modeler believes about this parameter. In camdl, model priors always optional. Parameters without priors are structural constants we may treat as known or fixed (population size, initial seed count) supplied via `--params` (and held fixed during inference). Models without any priors are valid for simulation, but they are doing so either at fixed parameter values or with implicit "flat" priors, which can lead to misleading inference and predictions when data is scarce. ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Supported prior distributions | Distribution | Syntax | Notes | |-----------------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------| | `log_normal` | `~ log_normal(mu = M, sigma = S)` | mu, sigma on the **log** scale | | `normal` | `~ normal(mu = M, sigma = S)` | mean, standard deviation | | `half_normal` | `~ half_normal(sigma = S)` | folded normal, support $[0,\infty)$ | | `beta` | `~ beta(alpha = A, beta = B)` | shape parameters | | `gamma` | `~ gamma(shape = K, rate = R)` | rate parameterization (not scale) | | `exponential` | `~ exponential(rate = R)` | rate = 1/mean | | `uniform` | `~ uniform(lower = L, upper = U)` | explicit uniform | All arguments are named (keyword), never positional. Arguments must be compile-time constants — arithmetic like `mu = log(0.3)` is fine. ::: ### Prior predictive checks Encoding priors in the model enables the first step of the model building dialogue: carrying our prior, highly-uncertain beliefs forward into simulation *without any data*. A **prior predictive check** draws parameter values from the prior, simulates the model at each draw, and examines the resulting distribution of outcomes. If the prior predictive distribution includes absurd epidemics — infecting the entire population in three days, or producing no infections at all — that's an early warning that the model is misspecified or our beliefs need revision. This check is only possible if we encode our beliefs as priors in the model; without them, there is nothing to simulate from. To see this concretely, consider our toy SIR with uniform priors — the "I have no idea" starting point: ```camdl parameters { beta : rate in [0.05, 1.0] ~ uniform(lower = 0.05, upper = 1.0) gamma : rate in [0.01, 0.5] ~ uniform(lower = 0.01, upper = 0.5) } ``` ::: {#9b33a7b8 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Both are simulated on the same toy SIR (N = 10,000). The uniform prior produces epidemics ranging from nothing to 8,000+ simultaneous infections; the log-normal prior concentrates mass in a more plausible range, but is still broad.](experiments_files/figure-html/fig-prior-predictive-comparison-output-1.png){#fig-prior-predictive-comparison width=1480 height=504} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-prior-r0 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Plotting code"} rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n_r0 = 10_000 # Uniform: beta ~ U(0.05, 1.0), gamma ~ U(0.01, 0.5) beta_u = rng.uniform(0.05, 1.0, n_r0) gamma_u = rng.uniform(0.01, 0.5, n_r0) r0_uniform = beta_u / gamma_u # Log-normal: beta ~ LN(-1.0, 0.5), gamma ~ LN(-2.0, 0.5) — no bounds clipping beta_ln = np.exp(rng.normal(-1.0, 0.5, n_r0)) gamma_ln = np.exp(rng.normal(-2.0, 0.5, n_r0)) r0_lognormal = beta_ln / gamma_ln # Total infections from prior predictive simulation summ_u = prior_summary(prior_uniform) summ_ln = prior_summary(prior_lognormal) fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5)) # Left: R0 distributions (log scale) bins_r0 = np.logspace(np.log10(0.1), np.log10(200), 60) ax1.hist(r0_uniform, bins=bins_r0, alpha=0.5, color="#cc3333", edgecolor="none", label=f"Uniform (median {np.median(r0_uniform):.1f})", density=True) ax1.hist(r0_lognormal, bins=bins_r0, alpha=0.5, color="#3366cc", edgecolor="none", label=f"Log-normal (median {np.median(r0_lognormal):.1f})", density=True) ax1.set_xscale("log") ax1.axvline(1.0, color=GREY, linestyle=":", alpha=0.5, linewidth=0.8) ax1.set_xlabel("Implied $R_0 = \\beta / \\gamma$") ax1.set_ylabel("Density") ax1.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9) ax1.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) # Right: total infections (decision-relevant outcome) ti_u = summ_u["total_infections"].to_numpy() ti_ln = summ_ln["total_infections"].to_numpy() bins_ti = np.linspace(0, max(ti_u.max(), ti_ln.max()) * 1.05, 35) ax2.hist(ti_u, bins=bins_ti, alpha=0.5, color="#cc3333", edgecolor="none", label="Uniform", density=True) ax2.hist(ti_ln, bins=bins_ti, alpha=0.5, color="#3366cc", edgecolor="none", label="Log-normal", density=True) ax2.set_xlabel("Total infections (of 10,000)") ax2.set_ylabel("Density") ax2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9) ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Implied R₀ and total infections under two priors. **Left:** R₀ = β/γ on a log scale (10,000 draws). The uniform prior spreads mass across two orders of magnitude — R₀ values of 50+ are not negligible. The log-normal prior concentrates around R₀ ≈ 3. The dotted line marks R₀ = 1 (epidemic threshold). **Right:** total infections from the prior predictive simulations (200 draws). The uniform prior produces everything from zero infections to total saturation; the log-normal prior concentrates in a narrower, more plausible range.](experiments_files/figure-html/fig-prior-r0-output-1.png){#fig-prior-r0 width=1480 height=500} ::: ::: | Prior | Peak infected (median, 95% range) | Total infections (median, 95% range) | |-------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------| | Uniform | 1178 (10–8641) | 7170 (3–9990) | | Log-normal | 2514 (10–6002) | 8914 (11–9987) | The uniform prior says every value of $\beta$ and $\gamma$ within the bounds is equally likely. This sounds "uninformative" but it's actually a strong statement: it implies that $R_0 = \beta / \gamma$ values of 50+ are just as plausible as $R_0 = 2$ (the log scale in the left panel makes this visible). Look at what this does to the *implied distribution of outcomes* in the right panel. The spike at zero total infections is the uniform prior telling you there is substantial probability that the epidemic doesn't happen at all — because a large fraction of the $(\beta, \gamma)$ draws produce $R_0 < 1$. If you're modeling an outbreak that observably infected 500 people, putting 20–30% of your prior mass on "no epidemic" is not uncertainty — it's incoherence. Your other beliefs (that flu is transmissible, that this is a boarding school, that an outbreak clearly occurred) are *mathematically incompatible* with the fizzle-out probability implied by uniform priors. The prior predictive makes this visible before you've touched any data. ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Coherence and the Dutch book The idea that beliefs must be internally consistent has deep roots. [Ramsey (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100011621) argued that a rational agent's degrees of belief must obey the probability axioms — otherwise an adversary can construct a set of bets (a "Dutch book") that guarantee the agent loses money regardless of the outcome. [De Finetti (1937)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02938457) formalized this: incoherent probabilities are operationally exploitable. What does this have to do with priors on $\beta$ and $\gamma$? The prior predictive is a *coherence audit*. Your prior over parameters *implies* a prior over outcomes — including the probability of epidemic fizzle-out. If you say "I'm uniform over ($\beta$, $\gamma$)" while simultaneously believing "an epidemic is underway," those two beliefs are incoherent: the first assigns ~25% probability to an event the second considers near-impossible. A Dutch book exists against you. The prior predictive makes this visible by computing the implied outcome distribution and letting you check it against your other knowledge before the data ever enters the picture. ::: The log-normal prior concentrates mass around more realistic values (median $\beta \approx 0.37$, median $\gamma \approx 0.14$, implying $R_0 \approx 2.7$) but is still quite broad — the 95% range of outcomes spans an order of magnitude. This is the "I think it's flu-like but I'm not very sure" prior. Better, but still too vague to be useful for a specific setting. ### From toy model to real data The prior predictive tells us something important: even our log-normal priors produce a wide range of outcomes. In practice, we'd know more — the pathogen, the population, the clinical picture. A boarding school flu outbreak in January is not a novel pathogen in a megacity. Let's ground the rest of this chapter in a real dataset: the [1978 English boarding school influenza outbreak](http://alun.math.ncsu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2017/01/influenza_78.pdf) (Anonymous, 1978, *BMJ* 1:578). This is literally the textbook SIR example — 763 boys at a boarding school in North England, 512 of whom were confined to bed with H1N1 influenza over 14 days in January 1978. The data is daily prevalence: how many boys were in bed each day. ::: {#cell-fig-boarding-school-data .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Plotting code"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5)) ax.bar(flu_data["day"], flu_data["in_bed"], width=0.8, color="#cc3333", alpha=0.7, edgecolor="none", label="Confined to bed") ax.bar(flu_data["day"], flu_data["convalescent"], width=0.8, bottom=flu_data["in_bed"], color="#f4a460", alpha=0.5, edgecolor="none", label="Convalescent") ax.set_xlabel("Day of outbreak") ax.set_ylabel("Number of boys") ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9) ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 13.5) ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The 1978 boarding school influenza outbreak. Daily prevalence (number of boys confined to bed) over 14 days. 512 of 763 boys were eventually infected — a 67% attack rate.](experiments_files/figure-html/fig-boarding-school-data-output-1.png){#fig-boarding-school-data width=1030 height=504} ::: ::: Now we can write an SIR model with *informed* priors — beliefs that reflect what was known about influenza in 1978. By then, decades of epidemiological study had established that influenza R0 typically falls between 1.5 and 4 ([Biggerstaff et al., 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4169819/)), with an infectious period of 2–5 days. In a boarding school with communal dining and dormitories, the reporting fraction (proportion confined to bed) would be high. These are genuine prior beliefs — not arbitrary numbers, but the accumulated knowledge of the field. ```camdl parameters { beta : rate in [0.1, 5.0] ~ log_normal(mu = log(2.0), sigma = 0.5) gamma : rate in [0.1, 1.0] ~ log_normal(mu = log(0.4), sigma = 0.3) N0 : count I0 : count rho : probability in [0.5, 1.0] ~ beta(alpha = 5.0, beta = 2.0) k : positive in [1.0, 100.0] ~ half_normal(sigma = 10.0) } ``` The log-normal on `beta` centers around 2.0 (giving R0 ≈ 5 with gamma ≈ 0.4 — high for flu, but a boarding school is a high-contact setting). The log-normal on `gamma` centers around 0.4 (infectious period ≈ 2.5 days). The beta prior on `rho` is skewed toward high values — in a boarding school, sick boys were conspicuous. ::: {#2c71bdc4 .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Compare to the vague-prior SIR above — the informed priors produce epidemics concentrated in the plausible range: peaks of 100–400 over 5–15 days, consistent with what we'd expect from flu in a school of 763.](experiments_files/figure-html/fig-boarding-school-prior-pred-output-1.png){#fig-boarding-school-prior-pred width=1030 height=504} ::: ::: The contrast with the vague-prior SIR is striking. Informed priors produce epidemics that look like flu in a school — peaks in the hundreds, durations of 1–2 weeks. The real data (black dots) falls within the prior predictive envelope, which is exactly what we want: our beliefs are consistent with the observed outbreak. If the data had fallen outside the envelope, we'd know our priors were wrong before even attempting inference. ::: {#cell-fig-boarding-school-prior-summary .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Plotting code"} rng_bs = np.random.default_rng(42) n_bs = 10_000 # Boarding school priors: beta ~ LN(log(2.0), 0.5), gamma ~ LN(log(0.4), 0.3) beta_bs = np.exp(rng_bs.normal(np.log(2.0), 0.5, n_bs)) gamma_bs = np.exp(rng_bs.normal(np.log(0.4), 0.3, n_bs)) r0_bs = beta_bs / gamma_bs bs_summ = prior_summary(bs_prior) fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5)) # Left: R0 bins_r0 = np.linspace(0, 25, 50) ax1.hist(r0_bs, bins=bins_r0, alpha=0.6, color="#cc3333", edgecolor="none", density=True) ax1.axvline(np.median(r0_bs), color="#cc3333", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label=f"Median R₀ = {np.median(r0_bs):.1f}") ax1.axvline(1.0, color=GREY, linestyle=":", alpha=0.5, linewidth=0.8) ax1.set_xlabel("Implied $R_0 = \\beta / \\gamma$") ax1.set_ylabel("Density") ax1.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9) ax1.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) # Right: total infections ti_bs = bs_summ["total_infections"].to_numpy() bins_ti = np.linspace(0, 763, 35) ax2.hist(ti_bs, bins=bins_ti, alpha=0.6, color="#cc3333", edgecolor="none") ax2.axvline(512, color="black", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Observed (512)") ax2.set_xlabel("Total infections (of 763)") ax2.set_ylabel("Frequency") ax2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9) ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Implied R₀ and total attack size under the informed boarding school priors. **Left:** R₀ = β/γ concentrates around 3–8, consistent with influenza in a high-contact setting (dashed line: median). **Right:** the stochastic model either fizzles (spike near zero — the index case recovers before transmitting) or produces a large outbreak. Even with known parameters, outcomes vary — and some outbreaks fail to take off entirely (the cluster near zero).](experiments_files/figure-html/fig-process-uncertainty-output-1.png){#fig-process-uncertainty width=1493 height=504} ::: ::: This is **process uncertainty**: even with the same parameters, the stochastic dynamics produce different outcomes each time. The grey spaghetti shows the range — most epidemics peak between 250 and 350 infected, but the timing and exact shape vary. Some outbreaks (the flat lines near zero) fail to take off entirely: with only one initial infection, there's a real chance the index case recovers before transmitting. The observed peak of 298 (dashed line) falls squarely within the distribution — the model is consistent with the data at these parameters. Notice how tight the process uncertainty is compared to the prior predictive spread. With 763 people, the law of large numbers is already working — the epidemic is "large enough" that individual-level stochasticity averages out. In smaller populations or with more heterogeneous contact patterns, process uncertainty would be much wider. In practice, transmission rates also fluctuate day-to-day due to environmental factors (school schedules, weather, gatherings). camdl supports this via `overdispersed()`, following [He et al. (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2009.0151) — we'll use it in the [He et al. vignette](../vignettes/he2010.qmd). Remember: we haven't fit to data yet. The parameters here ($\beta = 1.66$, $\gamma = 0.44$) are textbook values from the literature, not posterior estimates. The 1978 data (black dots) is overlaid for orientation — to check that the model *can* produce trajectories consistent with reality at these values. Actual parameter estimation comes in [Fitting to Data](fitting.qmd). ## The observation process — what the data actually looks like Everything so far has shown the *true* infected count $I(t)$ — the model's internal state. We introduced the observation model in [Building an SIR Model](getting-started.qmd): the pipeline of reporting fraction $\rho$ and negative binomial noise that stands between the true epidemic and your data. That chapter used `incidence(infection)` — accumulated new cases per observation window. The boarding school model uses `prevalence(I)` instead, because the data is a daily bed count: how many boys are confined *right now*, not how many became infected since last week. ```camdl observations { in_bed : { projected = prevalence(I) every = 1 'days likelihood = neg_binomial(mean = rho * projected, r = k) } } ``` The observation process adds a third layer of uncertainty on top of parameter and process uncertainty. The red line is the true $I(t)$ — the model's internal state. The dashed line is $\rho \cdot I(t)$, the expected observation. The grey dots are 20 independent draws from the negative binomial observation model: each is what a hypothetical dataset *could* look like from this one epidemic. The red line is one realization. The grey dots are observations from that realization. Inference must work backwards from a single set of noisy observations to recover both the process trajectory and the underlying parameters — bridging all three layers of uncertainty simultaneously. ## What's next The three layers of uncertainty — parameter, process, and observation — are the foundation everything else builds on. In the [next chapter](scenarios.qmd), we'll put them to work: interventions that modify the model mid-simulation, scenarios that package counterfactual comparisons, parameter sweeps that test robustness, and a batch system that manages it all reproducibly.
